strengths.quote: The absence of a route is a feature of the document’s attention, not a map of the event.
strengths.why: Chapter 6 makes a sharp, memorable distinction between documentary silence and historical reality.

strengths.quote: A rider can cross open ground quickly; an empire has to make messages arrive.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 compresses the transition from mobile force to administration into an elegant hinge.

weaknesses.quote: The relation between frontier mobility and aggression remains open, but it can be made more exact.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 6 begins an extended synthesis after the core Lindisfarne analysis has already landed, producing a recap loop.

weaknesses.quote: The passage does not establish that the proposal was put into operation or that a station actually drew labour and animals from those units.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7 handles uncertainty responsibly, but variants of this qualification recur so often that they slow the argument.

chapterNotes.6: A focused source reading of Alcuin distinguishes moral interpretation, material aid, and absent military detail with unusual care. Its late comparison with the Mongol material is conceptually useful but repetitive and slightly blurs the chapter boundary.
chapterNotes.7: The chapter develops a coherent sequence from genealogy and coalition to Ögedei’s proposed communications system, then to conquest, succession, and fragmentation. Concrete mechanisms and careful attribution are strong; repeated caveats about proposal versus implementation and several closing restatements reduce momentum.

strengths.quote: Subduing and allying are different verbs, and the narrative requires both.
strengths.why: Chapter 6 clearly preserves the distinction between coercion and coalition rather than flattening incorporation into consent.

strengths.quote: The proposed network translates distance into a series of exchanges governed by place, personnel, and horses.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 turns an abstract claim about imperial reach into a specific administrative mechanism.

weaknesses.quote: The relation between frontier mobility and aggression remains open, but it can be made more exact.
weaknesses.why: In Chapter 6 this introduces yet another synthesis after extensive Temüjin, Lindisfarne, Ögedei, and Wells sections, prolonging a chapter already covering most of the next chapter’s ground.

weaknesses.quote: The verdict is narrower than either “mobility caused Mongol violence” or “administration civilised conquest.”
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7 arrives at a sound qualification, but it repeats distinctions already developed at length in Chapter 6 and earlier in this chapter.

chapterNotes.6: This version adds substantial Temüjin, Ögedei, and Wells discussion before and around the complete Lindisfarne analysis, so its comparative thesis is explicit and evidence-rich. Because Chapter 7 then repeats the same Mongol arc, Chapter 6 feels overextended and weakens progression across the excerpt.
chapterNotes.7: The text is identical to A’s Chapter 7 and retains its strong causal distinctions, vivid hinge sentences, and responsible treatment of source limits. In B’s sequence, however, its content has already been extensively previewed in Chapter 6, making the reading experience markedly more redundant.

reason: A preserves the excerpt’s substantive arguments while assigning Lindisfarne primary weight in Chapter 6 and the detailed Mongol analysis to Chapter 7. B offers a fuller comparative Chapter 6, but nearly all of that added Temüjin, Ögedei, and Wells material reappears in its identical Chapter 7; the result is weaker chapter differentiation, slower pacing, and more recap. A’s greater polish does not increase certainty: it repeatedly preserves the limits of Alcuin’s evidence and the proposal-versus-implementation uncertainty in the Mongol source.
remainingProblems: Both versions repeatedly restate that Alcuin’s letter cannot establish the raiders’ organisation.
Both versions overuse symmetrical caution about what sources establish and do not establish, which sometimes makes the prose feel procedurally uniform.
Chapter 7 in both versions circles its central distinction between conquest and administration through several conclusions before ending.
